A SELLER-SIDE BROKER’S DUTY TO INSPECT AND DISCLOSE (CIV. CODE §§ 2079-2079.7; EASTON V. STRASSBURGER) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528 · Contra Costa County

WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This information sheet describes one specific duty California law places on the real estate broker or salesperson who is working for the seller of a home: the duty to conduct a reasonably competent and diligent visual inspection of the property offered for sale and to disclose to a prospective buyer what that inspection would reveal. It also describes the boundaries the Legislature and the Court of Appeal have drawn around that duty. It is being prepared in connection with the property at 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528 in Contra Costa County, a transaction in which Leticia Marks was the prospective buyer, Dana and Paul Reyes was the seller, and Valley Ridge Realty, Inc. acted as the broker or salesperson on the selling side. The condition or fact recorded as being at issue is: Cracked slab and sloping floors in the rear addition, and earth movement on the downhill slope. Each clause below reports what a named Civil Code section or a named published California opinion says — where the duty came from, which properties and transactions the statutes reach, what standard of care applies, what the inspection does not have to include, what a broker may do with information the seller supplies, what duty of care the buyer keeps, how long the statute allows an action for breach of the duty to be commenced, how the duty of a buyer’s own broker differs, and which other disclosure duties this article leaves untouched. This sheet does not evaluate the transaction at 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528, does not decide whether anything recorded above happened or whether any duty was breached, and does not tell anyone what to do.

THE STATUTORY DUTY (CIV. CODE § 2079)
Civil Code section 2079 states the duty in a single sentence. Subdivision (a) provides that it is the duty of a licensed real estate broker or salesperson, "to a prospective buyer of residential real property improved with one to four dwelling units or a manufactured home as defined in Section 18007 of the Health and Safety Code, to conduct a reasonably competent and diligent visual inspection of the property offered for sale and to disclose to that prospective buyer all facts materially affecting the value or desirability of the property that an investigation would reveal, if that broker has a written contract with the seller to find or obtain a buyer or is a broker who acts in cooperation with that broker to find and obtain a buyer." Three features of that sentence are on its face. The duty is owed to a prospective buyer, not to a client, so it exists without any contract between the broker and the buyer. It attaches to the broker who holds a written contract with the seller and also to a cooperating broker who works with that broker to find and obtain a buyer. And it has two halves — an inspection and a disclosure of what an investigation would reveal. Subdivision (b) adds a second duty, owed by the same licensees, "to comply with this section and any regulations imposing standards of professional conduct adopted pursuant to Section 10080 of the Business and Professions Code with reference to Sections 10176 and 10177 of the Business and Professions Code." The section as quoted here is the version amended by Stats. 2019, Ch. 310, Sec. 8 (AB 892), effective January 1, 2020. Whether Valley Ridge Realty, Inc. stood in either of the two relationships the section describes, and what an inspection of 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528 would have revealed, are questions of fact this sheet does not reach.

WHERE THE DUTY CAME FROM: EASTON V. STRASSBURGER AND THE LEGISLATURE’S RESPONSE
The duty began as a judicial decision. In Easton v. Strassburger (1984) 152 Cal.App.3d 90, a buyer purchased a Diablo property built partly on uncompacted fill; earth movement after the sale damaged the house, and the listing brokerage’s agents had inspected the property several times without testing or reporting the soil. The Court of Appeal held that a seller’s broker’s duty to disclose "includes the affirmative duty to conduct a reasonably competent and diligent inspection of the residential" property "listed for sale and to disclose to prospective purchasers all facts materially affecting the value or desirability of the property that such an investigation would reveal." Actual knowledge was not required: the court reviewed evidence that the agents had seen what the opinion calls "red flags" — netting on a repaired slope, a guest-house floor out of level — and concluded that "The jury merely had to conclude—as apparently it did—that a reasonably competent and diligent inspection of the property would have uncovered the past history of soils problems." The Legislature answered in 1985 by adding the article that now contains sections 2079 through 2079.25. That article carries its own statement of intent in section 2079.12: subdivision (b) says "It is the intent of the Legislature to codify and make precise the holding of Easton v. Strassburger, 152 Cal. App. 3d 90. It is not the intent of the Legislature to modify or restrict existing duties owed by real estate licensees." Subdivision (a)(4) says "That Sections 2079 to 2079.6, inclusive, of this article should be construed as a definition of the duty of care found to exist by the holding of Easton v. Strassburger, 152 Cal. App. 3d 90, and the manner of its discharge, and is declarative of the common law regarding this duty." Nothing in Easton or in section 2079.12 is specific to 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528.

WHICH PROPERTIES AND TRANSACTIONS THE ARTICLE REACHES (CIV. CODE §§ 2079, 2079.1, 2079.6)
The article’s reach is set by three provisions. Section 2079 itself names the property: residential real property improved with one to four dwelling units, or a manufactured home as defined in Health and Safety Code section 18007. Section 2079.1 extends the article beyond outright sales, providing that "The provisions of this article relating sale transactions of residential real property comprising one to four dwelling units apply with equal force to leases of that property that include an option to purchase, ground leases of land on which one to four dwelling units have been constructed, or real property sales contracts, as defined in Section 2985, for that property." Section 2079.6 carves out certain subdivision sales: the article "does not apply to sales which are required to be preceded by the furnishing, to a prospective buyer, of a copy of a public report pursuant to Section 11018.1 or Section 11234 of the Business and Professions Code and sales that can be made without a public report pursuant to Section 11010.4 of the Business and Professions Code, unless the property has been previously occupied." Whether the transaction involving 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528 falls inside or outside those descriptions is a question of fact and law this sheet does not answer.

THE STANDARD OF CARE, AND THE WORD "VISUAL" (CIV. CODE § 2079.2)
Section 2079.2 defines how well the inspection must be done: "The standard of care owed by a broker under this article is the degree of care that a reasonably prudent real estate licensee would exercise and is measured by the degree of knowledge through education, experience, and examination, required to obtain a license under Division 4 (commencing with Section 10000) of the Business and Professions Code." The measure is therefore the licensee’s own professional knowledge, not that of an engineer, a contractor or a home inspector. The kind of inspection required is also narrower than the word Easton used. In Field v. Century 21 Klowden-Forness Realty (1998) 63 Cal.App.4th 18, the Court of Appeal put it directly: "Section 2079 statutorily limits the duty of inspection recognized in Easton to one requiring only a visual inspection." The same opinion notes that "the statutory scheme expressly states a selling broker has no obligation to purchasers to investigate public records or permits pertaining to title or use of the property." What a reasonably prudent licensee would have seen at 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528 is a question of fact outside this sheet.

WHAT THE INSPECTION DOES NOT INCLUDE (CIV. CODE § 2079.3; WILSON V. CENTURY 21 GREAT WESTERN REALTY)

Wilson v. Century 21 Great Western Realty (1993) 15 Cal.App.4th 298 applied those limits to a house whose foundation lacked steel reinforcement and anchor bolts. INFORMATION THE SELLER SUPPLIES: ROBINSON V. GROSSMAN
A recurring question is what a seller’s agent must do with statements the seller makes about the property. In Robinson v. Grossman (1997) 57 Cal.App.4th 634, buyers argued that the disclosure half of section 2079 carried with it a duty either to verify the seller’s information independently or to disclaim knowledge of its accuracy. The Court of Appeal rejected that reading: "We find no support for the Robinsons’ argument section 2079’s disclosure duty includes a duty to independently verify or disclaim the accuracy of the seller’s representations, and we do not interpret section 2079 in that manner." The court described what the statute does require of the seller’s agent: "In making the required disclosures, the sellers’ agent is required only to act in good faith and not convey the seller’s representations without a reasonable basis for believing them to be true." It also described where the burden then falls: "under the post-Easton statutory scheme, once the sellers and their agent make the required disclosures, it is incumbent upon the potential purchasers to investigate and make an informed decision based thereon." What Dana and Paul Reyes told Valley Ridge Realty, Inc. about 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528, and what basis there was for believing it, are facts outside this sheet.

Summer (2010) 188 Cal.App.4th 1510, buyers agreed to pay $749,000 for a property carrying $1,141,000 in deeds of trust; the court observed that real estate agents and brokers "have been held to have a duty to disclose matters that do not pertain to physical defects, but otherwise affect the desirability of the purchase", framed the question before it as "Here, we have at issue the duty of the brokers to disclose an impediment to the ability of the seller to convey title free and clear of monetary liens and encumbrances", and reversed a judgment for the brokers, "holding that, under the facts of this case, the brokers were obligated to disclose to the buyers that there was a substantial risk that the seller could not transfer title free and clear of monetary liens and encumbrances." Which duties, if any, were owed in the transaction at 318 Lark Hill Rd., Diablo, CA 94528 is not addressed here.
